svg.aria-label: Diagram: system-assigned against user-assigned managed identities in Azure, showing the differences in creation, lifecycle and sharing, the role-assignment arithmetic that makes user-assigned the default recommendation, the roughly 24-hour managed identity token cache that makes Entra groups unsuitable for changing a managed identity's permissions, the orphaned role assignments left behind when an identity is deleted, and the rule that whoever can run code on a resource holds every permission its identities have
svg.title: Managed identities cost nothing in money — the two prices are a 24-hour token cache and role assignments nothing cleans up
svg.text: The identity with no credential, no licence and no cost. It still has two prices.
Neither is money. One is a cache you cannot flush; the other is a pile of role assignments nothing deletes for you.
Two types, and the three differences that decide between them
System-assigned
User-assigned
Creation
part of an Azure resource
a stand-alone Azure resource
Life cycle
shared — “when the parent resource is
deleted, the managed identity is deleted”
independent — “must be explicitly
deleted”, even with nothing attached
Sharing
“Can’t be shared” — one resource only
“Can be shared” across many resources
Microsoft’s own default: user-assigned identities are “the recommended managed identity type for Microsoft services”.
The arithmetic behind that recommendation
Four virtual machines needing the same two targets. With a system-assigned identity each, that is
4 × 2 = 8 role
assignments
to create and maintain. With one shared user-assigned identity,
— against the 4,000 per-scope budget of post #18.
Price one: a cache you cannot flush
“The back-end services for managed identities maintain
a cache per resource URI for around 24 hours.”
“It can take several hours for changes to a managed
identity’s group or role membership to take effect.”
“It isn’t possible to force a managed identity’s token
to be refreshed before its expiry.”
So the group-based pattern of posts #19 and #32 does
not work here. Grant permissions on the identity, and
use the user-assigned identity as the group instead.
Price two: assignments nothing removes
“Role assignments aren’t automatically deleted when
either system-assigned or user-assigned managed
identities are deleted.”
They must be deleted by hand “so the limit of role
assignments per subscription isn’t exceeded”. In the
portal they read “Identity not found”.
And a deleted system-assigned identity “counts
towards your limit until fully purged after 30 days” —
so churn in ephemeral compute meets a rate limit, and
the request “fails with an HTTP 429 error”.
Who really holds the permissions, and when system-assigned is still right
The privilege travels with the code
“If a user has access to install or execute code on this
resource, then the user has access to all the identities
assigned/associated to the Azure resource.”
And whoever may assign the identity “can assign it to a
different Azure resource and have access to all the
permissions available to the managed identity.”
Same shape as post #33. Neither appears in a role list.
The two cases that still want system-assigned
Audit logging
“If you need to log which specific resource carried out
an action, rather than which identity.”
Permissions lifecycle management
“If you require that the permissions for a resource be
removed along with the resource.”
A resource can hold both types at once.
Sources: Managed identities for Azure resources, and Best practice recommendations for managed identities, on Microsoft Learn.
